deep.reconstruction:
This page is a single drawing made on recycled IBM line-printer paper. The printed header is a trivial JCL job ('//CRAY2 JOB ... // EXEC PGM=IEFBR14'; IEFBR14 is the do-nothing program) and has no mathematical content.

How many curves there are. The machine transcription says four curves, but tracing the image shows three. There are six blue-marked ends, which gives three arcs, each running from the edge of the region to the edge.

(L) The nearly straight curve runs from the bottom-left end (~530,1150) up to the top-right end (~1610,200).

(C) The second curve starts at the top-right end (~1365,110). It descends steeply, turns near the right (the '+' at ~1550,630) and comes back leftward along a wavy path. It finally leaves at the lower-left end (~395,985).

(B) The third curve starts at the top-left end (~655,180) and goes down. It then makes a big loop: down and right to the bottom '+', up the right side, back left along the top arc (the '+' at ~920,385). It recrosses itself at ~(670,475) and leaves at the left end (~350,790).

The resulting configuration has 7 crossings:
- one self-crossing of B;
- B×L twice;
- B×C twice;
- C×L twice.

So every pair of curves meets twice, not once. In the plane drawing this is therefore not a pseudoline arrangement in the usual sense. In a pseudoline arrangement each pair meets exactly once and there are no self-crossings.

Markings at the crossings. At each of the 7 crossings Grothendieck draws two small black arrows, one tangent to each branch. A small blue arc marks the angular sector between them. This records a local oriented frame, or a chosen quadrant, at every double point.

Signs on the edges. The edges between consecutive crossings carry signs + or −.
- Along L the signs alternate: +, −, + between its successive crossings.
- Along C they also alternate: +, −, +.
- Along B the sequence is −, −, +, −, +. The alternation breaks around the loop and the self-crossing.

The blue strokes at the six ends look like a choice of side or orientation at infinity for each curve.

The most plausible reading is a test configuration. Grothendieck seems to be checking a local sign/orientation calculus on curve systems more general than pseudoline arrangements:
- curves meeting more than once;
- a self-intersecting curve;
- possibly read in the projective plane or the Möbius band, where pseudolines are one-sided.

The aim would be to see how edge signs and crossing frames propagate, and where consistency fails. The parity break along the looped curve may be exactly the phenomenon being tested. The following page (D, D′, x, y, hatched regions, local moves) supports a context of local manipulations of pseudoline systems. The exact meaning of the signs (curvature/convexity relative to the marked side, side of a reference line, or a coorientation parity) cannot be determined from this page alone. There is no text.
errors: No mathematical claim is written, so nothing can be checked for correctness. The edge signs along the self-intersecting curve do not follow the alternation seen on the other two curves. This may be intentional (the effect of the loop or self-crossing) or a slip; the page does not say.

ideas.what: A system of three curves, each pair crossing twice and one curve with a self-crossing, decorated with oriented tangent frames at the crossings and ± signs on the edges. It apparently serves as a test or counterexample configuration for a sign/orientation calculus on pseudoline-type systems.
ideas.modern_name: Decorated curve arrangements / immersed arcs with crossing data; local sequences and orientation (chirotope-like) data of arrangements; non-pseudoline curve systems
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pseudoline arrangements: Levi (1926), Ringel (1956), Goodman–Pollack (1980s); signed and oriented data: oriented matroid theory (Folkman–Lawrence 1978, Bland–Las Vergnas)

deep.surprise_reason: A wordless exploratory sketch: a test configuration of curves with crossing frames and edge signs. No statement can be extracted, and the sign rule cannot even be determined from this page. It belongs to the known but unpublished pseudoline dossier and shows nothing beyond working material.
transcription_corrections: There are three curves, not four. The six blue-marked ends determine three arcs; the near-straight one runs from about (530,1150) to (1610,200).
There are 7 crossings: one self-crossing of the looped curve, and each pair of distinct curves crosses twice.
The edge signs read along the curves are: straight curve +, −, +; second curve +, −, +; looped curve −, −, +, −, +. The flat list in the transcription does not reflect this placement.
Blue small arcs at each crossing mark the angular sector between the two black tangent arrows. The blue strokes at the six curve ends are separate markings.
The printed header is a JCL listing (IEFBR14 null job) on recycled printer paper, unrelated to the mathematics.
